Circle hypothesis of a crime series

Source: R/rtm.R
crchyp.Rd

Canter and Larkin's (1993) circle hypothesis: draw the circle whose diameter joins the two crime sites of a series that lie farthest apart. An offender whose home lies within it is a "marauder" (who travels out from home), one whose home lies outside a "commuter". Gives the circle, the share of the sites it holds (all of them, unless the series is far from round) and, for each home given, whether it lies within.

Usage

crchyp(x, y, home = NULL)

Arguments

x, y

The coordinates of the crime sites: finite numbers, at least two sites, in a planar projection (metres, feet).

home

NULL, or the home of the offender: c(x, y), or a matrix of two columns with one row per candidate home.

Value

A list: centre (x and y), r the radius, pair the two sites (row numbers) on the diameter, share the share of the sites within the circle, and mar, NULL or for each home TRUE when it lies within (a marauder).

Details

Of several pairs equally far apart, the first in the order of the sites is used. A point lies within the circle when its distance from the centre is at most \(r + 10^{-12} \max(1, r)\).

References

Canter, D. and Larkin, P. (1993). The environmental range of serial rapists. Journal of Environmental Psychology, 13(1), 63-69. doi:10.1016/S0272-4944(05)80215-4

Examples

crchyp(c(0, 4, 2), c(0, 0, 1), home = c(2, -1))
#> $centre
#> x y 
#> 2 0 
#> 
#> $r
#> [1] 2
#> 
#> $pair
#> [1] 1 2
#> 
#> $share
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $mar
#> [1] TRUE
#>
